# Designing for the Heat: How Cities Can Make Summer More Bearable

Every summer, the same photographs circulate: a thermal image of a city showing a dense red core bleeding into cooler green suburbs, or a sidewalk thermometer reading 120°F. These images illustrate a well-documented phenomenon called the urban heat island effect. Cities are built from asphalt, concrete, dark rooftops, and steel—all materials that absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night. Add cars, air conditioners pumping hot exhaust into streets, and the loss of vegetation, and a city can run ten to fifteen degrees Fahrenheit hotter than its surrounding countryside. As climate change makes heat waves longer, more frequent, and more lethal, this temperature gap is no longer a matter of comfort. Heat is already the deadliest weather hazard in the United States, killing more people in a typical year than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined. The good news is that urban heat is, to a large extent, a design problem—and design problems can be solved. The harder question is not whether cities can cool themselves, but who pays the costs and who reaps the benefits.

## The Case of the Trees

The single most effective and beloved intervention is also the oldest: planting trees. A mature shade tree can lower the surface temperature beneath it by twenty to forty degrees Fahrenheit, and through evapotranspiration—the process by which leaves release water vapor—it cools the surrounding air as well. Trees also absorb stormwater, filter pollution, and improve mental health. Medellín, Colombia, offers the most celebrated proof of concept. Between 2016 and 2019, the city built thirty "green corridors," planting some 8,800 trees and 350,000 shrubs along roads and waterways that had been barren concrete canyons. City officials measured temperature reductions of around 2°C in the corridors, and residents reported the streets felt dramatically more livable. Singapore, facing a tropical climate that will only intensify, has gone further, mandating greenery in new developments and draping buildings with vertical gardens.

Yet trees come with real tradeoffs. They take five to fifteen years to provide meaningful shade, meaning today's planting is a gift to future residents. They require water—an increasingly scarce commodity in cities like Phoenix and Los Angeles, where some drought-tolerant species provide little canopy. Their roots crack sidewalks and their limbs fall in storms, creating liability. And perhaps most consequentially, tree planting is not distributed equitably. In many American cities, a map of canopy cover is nearly a mirror image of a map of redlining: formerly redlined neighborhoods, disproportionately home to Black and Latino residents, can have half the tree cover of wealthier white neighborhoods. Medellín's corridors were deliberately routed through poor neighborhoods, but when cities green wealthy or gentrifying areas first, rising property values can push out the very residents the trees were meant to serve—a phenomenon researchers call "green gentrification." The lesson is not to plant fewer trees, but to plant them where the need is greatest and to pair greening with housing protections.

## Streets Built for Shade

Street design shapes heat as much as vegetation does. Wide, asphalt-heavy corridors optimized for car throughput function like frying pans. Cities can fight back with "cool pavements"—light-colored coatings that reflect rather than absorb sunlight. Phoenix, the hottest large city in America, has coated miles of streets with a sealant that keeps surfaces ten to twelve degrees cooler; Los Angeles has run similar pilots. The catch is that reflective pavement can bounce radiation back at pedestrians, making a person standing on the street feel warmer even as the surface cools. Cool pavement helps most at night, when it releases less stored heat, but it is no substitute for shade.

Better street design means narrowing roads, extending curbs, adding shade structures, canopies, and awnings, and orienting new development to create continuous shaded walking routes. Paris, facing brutal heat waves like the one that killed thousands of Europeans in 2003, has been converting schoolyards from asphalt into green spaces and opening "cool islands"—parks, museums, and air-conditioned public buildings—where residents can take refuge. The city has also experimented with car-free zones that reduce both engine heat and the asphalt devoted to vehicles. Here again, tradeoffs surface: narrowing roads to plant trees or widen sidewalks means removing parking or traffic lanes, which provokes fierce resistance from drivers and merchants who fear losing customers. The evidence from cities like New York and Barcelona suggests pedestrianized, shaded streets often boost local commerce, but the transition is politically painful, and cities that ignore the concerns of commuters risk backlash that undoes the whole project.

## Housing as Climate Infrastructure

The building where a person lives can matter more than the street outside. Much of the death toll from heat waves—famously in Chicago in 1995, when more than 700 people died, and in Paris in 2003—occurs indoors, among elderly and isolated residents in unventilated apartments. Housing policy is therefore heat policy. The most cost-effective building intervention is the cool roof: painting rooftops white or installing reflective materials can lower indoor temperatures significantly at minimal cost. New York City has coated millions of square feet of rooftop through volunteer programs. Insulation, window shading, cross-ventilation, and ceiling fans are cheap and effective; the tragedy is that they are least common in the aging, poorly maintained housing stock occupied by low-income renters.

This points to the central equity problem: air conditioning is the most reliable protection against heat death, but it is expensive to buy and run, and it feeds the very problem it solves by dumping heat into streets and straining electrical grids. Some jurisdictions have responded with law. A growing number of cities and states treat air conditioning as a habitability requirement, like heat in winter, and several utilities have been barred from shutting off power during heat waves. Phoenix and other cities have adopted "cooling center" networks and, more recently, paid tree-planting and weatherization programs targeted at the hottest, poorest neighborhoods, identified through community heat-mapping campaigns in which residents drive sensors through their own streets. The tradeoff is fiscal: retrofitting housing at scale costs billions, and without rent stabilization, upgraded buildings can become unaffordable to their current tenants.

## Transit and the Journey Through Heat

Public transit sits at the intersection of these issues. A person waiting fifteen minutes for a bus on an unshaded median in 105°F heat is experiencing a design failure. Cities can build shaded shelters—better still, air-conditioned ones, as Dubai does with its bus stations—plant trees at stops, and increase frequency so waiting time shrinks.
